rationale: Switch the features from the referential montage to the 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage, band-passed to 0.5–30 Hz. Neonatal seizures are focal and low-amplitude, and in a referential montage the shared reference signal and slow drift/high-frequency artifacts swamp the local rhythmic discharge. Bipolar derivations bring out local activity and remove the common-reference signal, which should make the per-channel max and median features much more seizure-specific.

I'm switching from the referential montage to the clinical neonatal bipolar double-banana montage (18 derivations of neighbouring electrodes). Neonatal seizures are focal and often low-amplitude. Subtracting neighbouring electrodes removes the activity shared through the common reference and makes local rhythmic discharges stand out more in the per-channel max and median features. Everything else stays the same, so any change in score comes from the montage alone.

I'm switching from the referential montage to the clinical neonatal bipolar double-banana (18 channels), with each channel band-pass filtered to 0.5–30 Hz and then downsampled to 64 Hz. Neonatal seizures are focal, so differences between neighbouring electrodes show local rhythmic discharges much better. Referential channels share a common reference plus slow drift and high-frequency noise, and those drown out low-amplitude focal seizures in the max/median channel features.

Seizures in neonates are focal, but the features are currently computed on the raw referential montage, where the shared reference, DC drift and 50 Hz mains noise dominate line length and RMS. This change switches to the clinical neonatal double-banana bipolar montage (18 derivations) with a 0.5–30 Hz zero-phase band-pass filter, so the per-channel features can pick up local rhythmic discharges.

I'm switching from the referential montage to the clinical 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage, with a 0.5–30 Hz zero-phase band-pass filter. Neonatal seizures are focal, and referential channels pick up the same common-reference and artifact signal everywhere, which hides local rhythmic discharges. Bipolar derivations cancel that shared signal, and the filter removes DC drift and high-frequency muscle noise before line length, RMS and band power are computed.

Background EEG amplitude and spectrum vary a lot between neonates, and the metric pools all seconds across neonates. So absolute log-power features mix up "this baby has a high-amplitude background" with "this second is a seizure". I'm keeping the raw features and adding a per-recording robust-normalized copy of each one: the feature minus the recording's median, divided by its IQR. This is label-free and computed inside `featurize`, so the classifier can detect seizures as departures from each neonate's own background.

Switch from the 19 referential channels to the 18-channel neonatal double-banana bipolar montage, band-passed to 0.5–30 Hz. Neonatal seizures are focal, so taking differences between neighbouring electrodes removes shared reference and common-mode noise that hide low-amplitude rhythmic discharges. The filter also removes drift and high-frequency artifact before line length, RMS and band powers are computed. I have not run this change, so I don't yet know how it changes the dev score.

Switch from the referential montage to the clinical 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage before computing features. Referential signals are dominated by activity shared with the reference electrode. Taking differences between neighbouring electrodes removes that shared activity, which brings out the focal, local rhythmic discharges typical of neonatal seizures and should give per-channel max/median features a much stronger signal.

Background EEG amplitude and spectrum vary a lot between neonates, so absolute log-power and line-length thresholds don't carry over well from one neonate to another. I'm keeping the raw features and adding a copy of each that is robust-standardized within its own recording (subtract the recording median, divide by the IQR, no labels used), so the GBM can pick up departures from that neonate's own background.

Neonatal seizures are focal, so local differences should show them more clearly. Everything else (8 s windows, features, gradient boosting, 10 s smoothing) is unchanged, so any score change comes from the montage. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a score for it yet.

This change adds per-recording robust z-scored copies of every feature, computed without labels (median and IQR over each recording's own seconds). The classifier can then pick up seizures as departures from that baby's own background, while the raw features stay available too.

The current features come from the 19 referential channels. A shared reference spreads artefacts and background across all of them, which hides focal, low-amplitude neonatal seizures. This change re-references to the 18-channel clinical double-banana bipolar montage and band-passes the signal to 0.5–30 Hz (removing DC drift and high-frequency muscle/line noise) before computing the same per-channel features, so the max over channels picks up local rhythmic discharges.

With a referential montage the shared reference signal and DC drift or line noise end up in every channel, which hides the focal, low-amplitude rhythmic discharges typical of neonatal seizures. Local bipolar derivations bring those discharges out, so the channel-max features should become much more discriminative.

Background EEG amplitude and spectra vary a lot between neonates, so absolute log-power and line-length thresholds don't carry over well from one neonate to another. This hurts a concatenated AUROC. This is label-free and done within each recording, so the classifier can tell seizures apart from that neonate's own baseline.
